dsa-sort-passes-01: Code har pass mein `a[i:]` ka minimum dhoondh ke slot i ke saath **swap** karta hai — shifting nahi. Sirf 2 passes chahiye.
Pass 1 (i = 0): poore array ka minimum index 0 pe aata hai. Pass 2 (i = 1): `a[1:]` ka minimum index 1 pe. Sirf swap hone wale do elements hilte hain.
Pass 1: min 4 (index 7) ↔ 29 → `[4, 13, 41, 7, 36, 18, 52, 29]`. Ab pass 2 tum karo. Trap: minima aage laake baaki ko right shift mat karo — 29 seedha index 7 pe gaya.
dsa-sort-passes-02: Insertion sort ka pass i sirf `a[i]` ko sorted prefix `a[:i]` mein daalta hai, aur loop i = 1 se start hota hai. 3 passes = i = 1, 2, 3.
3 passes ke baad sirf `a[:4]` (29, 13, 41, 7) sorted hoga; index 4 onwards (36, 18, 52, 4) bilkul untouched rahega.
i = 1: 13 insert → `[13, 29, 41, ...]`; i = 2: 41 already bada, no move. Ab i = 3 pe 7 ko insert karo. Trap: pehle element ko pass 1 mat gino.
dsa-sort-passes-03: Har option ek algorithm ka 2-pass state claim karta hai. Teeno sorts ko `[38, 12, 55, 21, 9, 47]` pe khud 2 passes tak trace karo aur option se milao.
Selection: pass i `a[i:]` ka min slot i pe swap karta hai (self-swap bhi ek pass hai). Insertion: pass i `a[i]` ko prefix mein daalta hai. Bubble: har sweep bacha hua largest end pe le jaata hai.
Bubble sweep 1 → `[12, 38, 21, 9, 47, 55]`; ye sirf 1 sweep hai, sweep 2 khud karo. Trap: selection pass 2 mein 12 already apni jagah hai — us self-swap pass ko skip mat karo.
dsa-sort-passes-04: Bubble sort bade elements ko right le jaata hai, par sawaal chhote element 3 ka hai jo left jaata hai. Socho: ek pass mein wo kitna khisak sakta hai?
Ek pass mein chhota element zyada se zyada ek slot left jaata hai (jab uske left wala bada ho aur us pe swap ho). 3 abhi 1-based position 6 pe hai.
Pass 1: `[8, 26, 14, 31, 3, 19, 22, 40]` — 3 ab position 5 pe. Passes 2 aur 3 khud karo. Trap: 3 ek hi pass mein front tak nahi pahunchta.
dsa-sort-passes-05: Given state `[2, 6, 9, 8, 1, 7]` mein sirf pehle 3 elements sorted hain aur 8, 1, 7 input jaise hi hain. Ye pattern kis sort ka 2-pass fingerprint hai?
2 passes ke baad: selection front pe do sabse chhote (1, 2) rakhta hai; insertion sirf `a[:3]` sort karta hai; bubble end pe do sabse bade (9, 8) rakhta hai.
Selection pass 1: min 1 ↔ 6 → `[1, 9, 2, 8, 6, 7]`, given se pehle hi alag. Ab insertion aur bubble ko 2 passes trace karo. Trap: sirf sorted prefix dekh ke selection mat bolo.
dsa-sort-passes-06: Ye selection sort ka ulta version hai: har pass `a[0..last]` ka **maximum** dhoondh ke `a[last]` se swap karta hai, yaani right end se fill karta hai.
Pass 1: last = 6, `a[0..6]` ka max. Pass 2: last = 5, `a[0..5]` ka max. Dono baar swap hai, shift nahi.
Pass 1: max 50 (index 5) ↔ 11 (index 6) → `[17, 42, 8, 33, 25, 11, 50]`. Ab last = 5 ke liye karo. Trap: max nikal ke baaki ko left shift mat karo.
dsa-sort-swaps-01: Sawaal swaps ka hai, comparisons ka nahi. Bubble sort ka har adjacent swap exactly ek inversion hatata hai.
Total swaps = inversions = pairs (i < j) jahan `a[i] > a[j]`. `[7, 3, 9, 1, 5, 2]` mein har element ke right mein usse chhote elements gino aur jodo.
7 ke right mein chhote: 3, 1, 5, 2 → 4. Ab 3, 9, 1, 5 ke liye gino. Trap: sirf input ke adjacent out-of-order pairs (7-3, 9-1, 5-2) mat gino.
dsa-sort-swaps-02: Swap line har pass mein chalti hai (6 passes), par sawaal sirf un passes ka hai jahan `m != i` — yaani minimum already slot i pe nahi tha.
Har i ke liye current `a[i:]` ka min dekho: agar wo already index i pe hai to self-swap (count nahi), warna real swap. Har pass ke baad array update karo.
i = 0: min 9 (index 3) ↔ 44 → `[9, 17, 62, 44, 30, 51, 26]`, real swap. i = 1: 17 already min, self-swap. Ab i = 2..5 khud karo. Trap: inversions mat gino.
dsa-sort-swaps-03: Sirf `a[j] > key` gino, `j >= 0` nahi. Har true comparison ek shift deta hai; ek extra (false) comparison tab hota hai jab loop `a[j] > key` fail hone se rukta hai.
Comparisons = shifts (= inversions) + un passes ki ginti jinka key index 0 tak nahi pahunchta. Keys 5, 18, 3, 15, 9 ko alag-alag dekho.
Inversions: 12 → {5, 3, 9} = 3, 18 → {3, 15, 9} = 3; 5 aur 15 ke khud gino. Trap: jo key front tak pahunchta hai, wahan loop `j >= 0` pe rukta hai — failing comparison nahi.
dsa-sort-swaps-04: Har statement ek counting rule hai — bubble swaps, selection swaps, selection comparisons, insertion comparisons. Ek-ek ko rule se check karo.

Rules: adjacent exchange ek inversion hatata hai; selection har pass mein ek swap statement chalata hai aur min-scan hamesha end tak jaata hai; insertion comparisons = inversions + (passes jo index 0 se pehle rukte hain).
Option C test karo: sorted `[1, 2, 3]` pe selection i = 0 mein j = 1, 2 dono check karta hai — scan rukta hai kya? D ke liye socho: jo key index 0 tak pahunchta hai, uska failing comparison hota hai?
dsa-sort-swaps-05: Shifts = inversions. Array do sorted halves hai: `2, 4, 6, 8` aur `1, 3, 5, 7`, to inversions sirf left-half element aur usse chhote right-half element ke beech hain.
Har right-half key ke liye gino: left half mein kitne elements usse bade hain. Total = in counts ka sum.
Key 1: 2, 4, 6, 8 sab bade → 4 shifts. Ab 3, 5, 7 ke liye gino. Trap: 4 × 4 = 16 mat lo — 2 < 3, 2 < 5 jaise pairs inversion nahi hain.
dsa-sort-swaps-06: Early-exit flag hai: loop tabhi rukta hai jab ek poora pass bina swap ke chale. Aur pass p sirf `n - 1 - p` pairs compare karta hai.
n = 8, to pass 0: 7 comparisons, pass 1: 6, pass 2: 5, ... Pehle dekho kis pass ke baad array sorted ho jaata hai, phir ek aur no-swap pass jodo.
Pass 0 trace karo: 3 > 1 swap, 3 > 2 swap, 3 < 6, 6 > 4 swap, ... End mein array sorted hai kya? Trap: sorted hone wale pass pe mat ruko — no-swap pass bhi ginta hai.
dsa-sort-props-01: Stable matlab equal keys apna input order rakhein. Har option mein dekho: kya koi element apne equal twin ko cross kar sakta hai?
Adjacent-swap sorts strict `>` ke saath equal neighbours ko kabhi swap nahi karte. Long-range swap, ya `>=` wala test, equal items ko cross kara sakta hai.
Selection ko `[3a, 3b, 1]` pe try karo: pass 1 mein min 1 ko index 0 pe swap karo — 3a kahan gaya? Trap: insertion mein `>` aur `>=` ka fark ignore mat karo.
dsa-sort-props-02: Selection sort long-range swap karta hai, isliye do 3 wale records ka order badal sakta hai. Strict `<` ka matlab: tie mein pehla mila minimum hi rehta hai.
4 passes (i = 0..3): har pass mein `a[i:]` ka pehla minimum dhoondh ke index i se swap karo. Har pass ke baad sequence likho aur (3,p), (3,r) ko track karo.
i = 0: min (1,q) index 1 pe → (3,p) se swap: `(1,q),(3,p),(3,r),(2,s),(1,t)`. Ab i = 1 se aage karo. Trap: selection ko stable maan ke 3s ka input order mat rakho.
dsa-sort-props-03: Input already sorted hai. Dekho kaunsa algorithm sorted input ka fayda utha ke jaldi khatam karta hai, aur kiske liye ye ulta worst case hai.
Sorted input mein inversions = 0. Yaad karo kis algorithm ka cost inversions pe depend karta hai, kiska inner loop hamesha poora chalta hai, aur last-element pivot ka split kaisa banta hai.
Quicksort test karo: `[1, 2, 3, 4]` pe pivot 4 → split 3 : 0, phir pivot 3 → 2 : 0 ... har level linear kaam. Trap: bina flag ka bubble sorted input pe bhi saare n - 1 passes chalata hai.
dsa-sort-props-04: Descending input insertion sort ka worst case hai: har key ko apne left ke saare elements ke past shift hona padta hai.
Pass i (i = 1..11) mein key i elements ke past jaata hai aur index 0 tak pahunchta hai, so koi failing comparison nahi. Total = $1 + 2 + \dots + 11$.
Pass 1: 1 comparison, pass 2: 2, ... Formula $\frac{(n-1)n}{2}$ mein n = 12 daalo. Trap: $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ mat lo — sum 11 tak jaata hai, 12 tak nahi.
dsa-sort-props-05: Keywords: **always** aur sirf O(n) inversions. Har sort ka cost kis cheez pe depend karta hai — inversions pe, ya kuch aur (jaise kisi element ko kitni door jaana hai)?
Insertion = Θ(n + I). Selection comparisons input se independent. Early-exit bubble ke passes = max leftward distance + 1. Flagless bubble har input pe saare passes chalata hai.
Bubble ke liye `[2, 3, ..., n, 1]` socho: sirf n - 1 inversions, par 1 ko kitne slots left jaana hai, aur ek pass use kitna le jaata hai? Trap: kam swaps ka matlab kam comparisons nahi.
dsa-sort-props-06: A mein bada 8 front pe hai, B mein chhota 1 end pe. Bubble mein bada element ek pass mein end tak pahunch jaata hai, chhota sirf ek slot left khisakta hai.
Passes = (sorted hone tak ke passes) + 1 no-swap confirming pass — lekin loop zyada se zyada n - 1 = 7 passes hi chalta hai.
A, pass 1: 8 end tak jaata hai → `[1, 2, ..., 8]`; flag ke hisaab se aur kitne passes? B mein 1 ko index 7 se 0 tak khud gino. Trap: loop limit ke baad extra confirming pass nahi hota.
dsa-sort-merge-01: Comparisons tabhi tak hote hain jab tak dono lists non-empty hain; ek list khaali hote hi doosri ke bache items bina comparison copy hote hain.
Dono fronts compare karo, chhota output mein, us list ka pointer aage. Sizes m = 4, n = 5, to count min(m, n) = 4 aur m + n - 1 = 8 ke beech hoga.
Shuruat: 3 vs 5 → 3; 8 vs 5 → 5; 8 vs 9 → 8. Aise hi gino jab tak koi list khaali na ho. Trap: end mein bache items (jaise 41) ke liye comparison mat gino.
dsa-sort-merge-02: Total = har merge ke comparisons ka sum, saare levels pe — size-1 pairs se final 4+4 merge tak. Actual count runs ke interleaving pe depend karta hai, formula pe nahi.
1+1 merges: 4 comparisons. `[3,14]+[9,22]`: 3 vs 9, 14 vs 9, 14 vs 22 → 3. Ab `[6,31]+[17,25]` aur final merge khud karo. Trap: worst-case formula $n\log_2 n - n + 1$ mat lagao.
dsa-sort-merge-03: Merge sort ka split position (mid) se hota hai, values se nahi. To sorted input pe recursion tree ka shape badalta hai kya?
$T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn$ ka recursion tree banao: levels kitne hain aur har level pe kitna kaam? Sorted input pe comparisons kam ho sakte hain, par copying ka kya?
Level 0: ek merge, n items copy. Level 1: do merges of n/2 — phir bhi total n copies. Ab levels gino. Trap: sorted input quicksort (end pivot) ka worst case hai, merge sort ka nahi.
dsa-sort-merge-04: Bottom-up mein ek pass poora level khatam karta hai: pass 1 size-1 runs (adjacent pairs) merge karta hai, pass 2 size-2 runs.
Pass 1: (27,10), (36,5), (18,41), (2,33) ko sort karo. Pass 2: pehle do size-2 runs ko merge karo, phir agle do — result do sorted blocks of 4.
Pass 1 → `[10, 27, 5, 36, 18, 41, 2, 33]`. Ab pass 2 mein `[10,27]+[5,36]` aur `[18,41]+[2,33]` merge karo. Trap: top-down ki tarah sirf left half pe mat ruko.
dsa-sort-merge-05: Char claims hain: stability, extra space, comparisons fixed hain ya nahi, aur best case. Har ek ko merge step ke behaviour se judge karo.
Tie pe left run se lena → earlier item pehle. Array merge ko temporary buffer chahiye. Ek merge ke comparisons min(m, n) se m + n - 1 tak vary karte hain; copying har level pe n items.
C test karo: `[1,2]+[3,4]` merge mein 2 comparisons, `[1,3]+[2,4]` mein 3 — same size, alag count? D ke liye socho: sorted input pe bhi har level n items copy hote hain ya nahi.
dsa-sort-merge-06: Maximum over all orderings matlab har merge ka worst case lo. Tree fix hai: 8 → 4 + 4 → 2 + 2 → 1 + 1.
Worst merge of m + n items = m + n - 1 comparisons. Merges: 4 of 1+1, 2 of 2+2, 1 of 4+4.
1+1 merges: 4 × 1 = 4. Ab 2+2 aur 4+4 waale khud lagao aur jodo. Trap: m + n mat lo — last bacha item hamesha free copy hota hai.
dsa-sort-quick-01: Lomuto partition: pivot = `a[hi]` = 14. i sirf tab badhta hai jab `a[j] <= 14`; aakhir mein pivot slot i + 1 pe jaata hai.
j = 0..6 chalo: `a[j] <= 14` ho to i += 1 aur `a[i] ↔ a[j]` (i == j ho to self-swap). Loop ke baad `a[i+1] ↔ a[7]`.
j = 0, 1: 12, 7 ≤ 14 → i = 0, 1, self-swaps. j = 2: 25 > 14, skip. Ab j = 3 se aage chalo. Trap: swap line 2 mat bhoolo — pivot a[i+1] se swap hota hai, a[i] se nahi.
dsa-sort-quick-02: Convention: swap line 1 ka har execution count hota hai (self-swaps bhi), plus swap line 2 hamesha ek baar. Pivot = 10.
Swap line 1 utni baar chalti hai jitne `a[j]` (j = 0..5) `<= 10` hain. Total swaps = wo count + 1.
4 ≤ 10 → i = 0 = j, self-swap (count). 9 ≤ 10 → i = 1 = j, self-swap. Ab 2, 11, 6, 15 check karo. Trap: comparisons (6) ko swaps mat samjho.
dsa-sort-quick-03: Sorted input + last-element pivot: har baar pivot subarray ka maximum hai, to split hamesha (k - 1) : 0 hota hai.
k items ka partition k - 1 comparisons karta hai. Calls ke sizes: 9, 8, ..., 2 (size 1 pe koi comparison nahi).
Pehli call: 9 items → 8 comparisons; doosri: 8 items → 7. Ab sab jodo. Trap: $1 + 2 + \dots + 9$ mat lo — size k pe k - 1 comparisons hain, k nahi.
dsa-sort-quick-04: Sorted input pe har `a[j] <= pivot` true hai, to swap line 1 har j pe chalti hai (i == j, self-swap) — aur convention unhe bhi ginta hai.
k sorted items ki call: swap line 1 → k - 1 baar, swap line 2 → 1 baar, total k swaps. Call sizes 9, 8, ..., 2.
Pehli call (k = 9): 8 self-swaps + 1 pivot swap = 9. Ab baaki calls ke liye jodo. Trap: sirf line 1 mat gino — har call swap line 2 bhi chalati hai.
dsa-sort-quick-05: Lomuto quicksort Θ(n²) tab hota hai jab baar-baar pivot ek end pe land kare (split n - 1 : 0). Har input ke liye socho pivot kahan girta hai.
Pivot = last element, test `<=`. Har input ke liye pivot ka rank dekho: max ya min ho to lopsided split. Random input pe expected split balanced hota hai.
All-equal `[5, 5, 5, 5]` try karo: har `a[j] <= 5` true, to i end tak jaata hai — pivot kahan aaya? Trap: descending ke liye sirf pehli call nahi, baad ki calls ka structure bhi dekho.
dsa-sort-quick-06: Ek partition ke baad pivot apni sorted position pe hota hai: left mein sab chhote, right mein sab bade. Har array mein aisa ek key dhoondo.
Keys 1..8 hain, to key k ki sorted position index k - 1 hai. Check: key k index k - 1 pe ho aur uske left ke saare keys < k (to right ke saare > k).
Pehle array mein index 3 pe 4 hai; left {3, 1, 2}, right {8, 6, 5, 7} — condition check karo. Trap: halves 'roughly split' dikhne se kaam nahi chalega; ek exact key chahiye.
dsa-sort-quick-07: Split 1 : 9 hai — unbalanced, par ratio constant hai. Aur quicksort dono parts pe recurse karta hai.
$T(n) = T(n/10) + T(9n/10) + cn$. Recursion tree mein har level ka total ≤ cn; ab depth nikalo.
Sabse lambi path har baar 9/10 hissa leti hai, to depth $\log_{10/9} n$. Ab is log ko $\log n$ se compare karo. Trap: unbalanced ≠ Θ(n²); wo sirf n - 1 : 0 jaise splits pe hota hai.
dsa-dc-recur-01: $T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n$: a = 3, b = 2, f(n) = n. Master theorem mein f(n) ko $n^{\log_b a}$ se compare karna hai.
f(n) = n ko $n^{\log_2 3}$ se compare karo. f chhota → leaves dominate, $\Theta(n^{\log_b a})$; barabar → ek extra $\log n$; bada → Θ(f(n)).
$\log_2 3$ approx karo: $2^1 = 2 < 3 < 4 = 2^2$, to exponent 1 aur 2 ke beech (≈ 1.585). Ab n se compare karo. Trap: exponent a/b = 3/2 nahi, $\log_b a$ hota hai.
dsa-dc-recur-02: a = 4, b = 2, f(n) = $n^2$. Pehle $n^{\log_b a}$ nikalo aur dekho f(n) usse chhota, barabar ya bada hai.
Master cases: f chhota → $\Theta(n^{\log_b a})$; f barabar → $\Theta(n^{\log_b a}\log n)$; f bada → Θ(f(n)). Yahan $\log_2 4$ nikalo.
Recursion tree level i: $4^i$ subproblems, har ek ka cost $(n/2^i)^2$. Level total simplify karo, phir $\log_2 n$ levels se multiply. Trap: log factor do baar mat lagao.
dsa-dc-recur-03: Har non-base call `f(n // 2)` ko **do** baar call karta hai (result reuse nahi hota). Sawaal total calls ka hai — internal aur leaf dono.
Calls: $C(n) = 1 + 2C(n/2)$, $C(1) = 1$. Ya recursion tree ke har level pe calls gino: n = 32, 16, 8, ..., 1.
Level 0: f(32) → 1 call; level 1: do f(16) → 2 calls; level 2: 4 calls ... f(1) wale level tak chalo aur jodo. Trap: sirf leaves f(1) mat gino.
dsa-dc-recur-04: Ab calls nahi, return value chahiye: $f(n) = 2f(n/2) + n$, $f(1) = 1$. Har internal call apna n add karta hai, leaves 1 return karte hain.
Recursion tree: level i pe $2^i$ calls, har ek $n/2^i$ add karta hai, to har internal level ka total 32. Internal levels (n ≥ 2) gino, aur leaves alag se jodo — har leaf 1 return karta hai.
Bottom-up chalo: f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2·1 + 2 = 4, f(4) = 2·4 + 4 = 12. Ab f(8), f(16), f(32) nikalo. Trap: leaves ke 1s mat chhodo.
dsa-dc-recur-05: Har recurrence alag type ka hai: master theorem, uneven split, ya subtract-by-one. Har ek ko solve karke dekho Θ(n log n) kaun deta hai.
Recursion tree socho: level cost × depth. Balanced ya constant-ratio split + linear combine → har level ≈ n, depth Θ(log n). T(n - 1) type mein depth n hoti hai.
C test karo: $2T(n/2) + n\log n$ mein level i ka cost $2^i \cdot \frac{n}{2^i}\log\frac{n}{2^i} = n\log\frac{n}{2^i}$ — ab levels pe sum karo. Trap: T(n - 1) + n ko n log n mat samjho.
dsa-dc-recur-06: Recurrence banao: 7 subproblems of size n/2, combine Θ(n²). To a = 7, b = 2, f(n) = n².
$n^{\log_2 7}$ ko n² se compare karo. f chhota → $\Theta(n^{\log_b a})$; barabar → × log n; bada → Θ(f(n)).
$\log_2 7$: $2^2 = 4 < 7 < 8 = 2^3$, to exponent 2 aur 3 ke beech — ab n² se bada hai ya chhota? Trap: plain block method ke 8 products mat socho; yahan 7 hain.
dsa-dc-recur-07: Har step n ko √n bana deta hai — n/2 se kahin tezi se chhota. Asli sawaal: kitni baar square root lene pe 2 tak pahunchte hain?
Example: $2^{16} → 2^8 → 2^4 → 2^2 → 2$, exponent har baar half. Ab S(m) solve karo aur m ko n mein wapas likho. Trap: √n ko n/2 jaisa mat treat karo.
dsa-graph-traverse-01: BFS: FIFO queue, poora level pehle, phir agla. Vertex enqueue hote hi marked, aur neighbours alphabetical order mein.
Figure se adjacency: A{B,C,E}, B{A,D,F}, C{A,G}, D{B,H}, E{A,F}, F{B,E,H}, G{C,H}, H{D,F,G}. Queue se nikalo, unmarked neighbours peeche daalo.
Dequeue A → [B, C, E]. Dequeue B → D, F add → [C, E, D, F]. Ab C se aage chalo. Trap: H ko F ke turant baad mat likho — jo pehle enqueue hua wahi pehle aata hai.
dsa-graph-traverse-02: Recursive DFS: alphabetically pehle unvisited neighbour pe turant jao; backtrack sirf tab jab current vertex ke saare neighbours visited hon.
Adjacency: A{B,C,E}, B{A,D,F}, C{A,G}, D{B,H}, E{A,F}, F{B,E,H}, G{C,H}, H{D,F,G}. Har step pe current vertex ka pehla unvisited neighbour lo.
A → B (A ka pehla) → D (B ka pehla unvisited) → H. Ab H se aage chalo. Trap: F se jaldi wapas mat jao — pehle dekho F ka koi neighbour abhi unvisited hai kya.
dsa-graph-traverse-03: Adjacency order kuch bhi ho sakta hai, to sirf DFS ka rule check karo: DFS kisi vertex ko tab tak nahi chhodta jab tak uska koi neighbour unvisited hai.
Edges: A-B, A-C, A-E, B-D, B-F, C-G, D-H, E-F, F-H, G-H. Har sequence mein current path (stack) rakho; agla vertex path ke sabse deep 'unfinished' vertex ka neighbour hona chahiye.
Last option test karo: A, B ke baad C aaya — tab B ke paas D ya F unvisited the kya? Baaki options bhi aise hi step-by-step check karo. Trap: BFS jaisa level order DFS order nahi hota.
dsa-graph-traverse-04: Adjacency order free hai, to BFS ka structure check karo: levels order mein, aur har dequeued vertex ke naye neighbours ek block mein, parents ke dequeue order mein.
Levels from A: L1 = {B, C, E}, L2 = {D, F, G}, L3 = {H}. B → D (aur F), C → G; F ka parent B ya E mein jo pehle dequeue ho.
Third option dekho: H (level 3) G (level 2) se pehle aa raha hai — BFS mein possible hai? Baaki options mein L2 ka order parents ke order se milao. Trap: L2 ke andar bhi order free nahi hai.
dsa-graph-traverse-05: Lists sort mat karo — stored order mein scan karna hai (0 ke liye pehle 2, phir 1). Aur driver 0 ke baad bache unvisited vertices pe DFS restart karta hai.
Recursive DFS: list ka pehla unvisited neighbour → recurse; dead end pe backtrack. Pehla tree khatam hone ke baad 1..6 mein jo unvisited bacha ho, wahan se restart.
0 → 2 (list [2, 1] ka pehla) → 4 (2 ki list [4, 1]) → 3. Ab 3 ki list [0, 5] se aage chalo. Trap: vertex 6 0 se reachable nahi — restart mat bhoolo.
dsa-graph-traverse-06: Queue ka size har step ke baad track karna hai. Dhyan: vertex pehle remove hota hai, phir uske neighbours add hote hain.
Adjacency: A{B,C,E}, B{A,D,F}, C{A,G}, D{B,H}, E{A,F}, F{B,E,H}, G{C,H}, H{D,F,G}. Har step ke baad queue contents likho aur max size note karo.
[A] → A remove, B, C, E add → [B, C, E]. Ab B remove karke uske unmarked neighbours add karo, aur aise hi aage. Trap: jo vertex process ho raha hai use queue mein mat gino.
dsa-graph-bfs-dist-01: BFS level = vertex 1 se fewest edges. DFS ka path shortest nahi hota. Vertex 9 sirf 8 se juda hai.
Level by level chalo: L0 = {1}, L1 = 1 ke neighbours, L2 = L1 ke naye neighbours, ... jab tak 9 na mile. Edges gino, vertices nahi.
L1 = {2, 3}, L2 = {4, 5}. Ab L3, L4, ... nikalo. Trap: path ke vertices mat gino, edges gino; aur 8 ka level 9 ka level nahi hai.
dsa-graph-bfs-dist-02: Vertices 1 se 12 tak hain. Jo vertex edge list mein kabhi nahi aata, wo bhi apna alag component hai.
Edges se groups banao: jude hue vertices ek set mein. Phir isolated vertices alag gino. n - m formula sirf forest (no cycle) pe chalta hai.
Groups: {1, 2, 3} (1-2, 2-3), {4, 5}. Ab 6-7-8 aur 9-10 dekho, phir bache vertices. Trap: 12 - 7 mat karo — 6-7-8 ek cycle hai.
dsa-graph-bfs-dist-03: Sirf ek statement **always** true hai. Har option BFS levels, DFS depth ya weighted graphs ke baare mein claim hai — har ek ka counterexample dhoondo.
Rule: jab u dequeue hota hai, uske har unvisited neighbour ko level d(u) + 1 milta hai. To kisi bhi edge ke do endpoints ke levels mein zyada se zyada kitna fark ho sakta hai?
Square graph s-a, s-b, a-c, b-c lo: d(a) = d(b) = 1, d(c) = 2, aur agar c ko a ne pakda to b-c non-tree edge hai. Ye kis option ko todta hai? Trap: DFS depth ko distance mat samjho.
dsa-graph-bfs-dist-04: n vertices, m edges, k components. Socho: c vertices wale component ko connected rehne ke liye minimum kitne edges chahiye? Saare options isi se judge hote hain.
Connected component with c vertices: kam se kam c - 1 edges, aur exactly c - 1 tabhi jab wo tree ho. Ise saare k components pe jodo. Extra edge cycle banata hai par k nahi badalta.
C ko triangle (n = 3, m = 3, k = 1) pe test karo: n - m kya aata hai? D: edge agar ek hi component ke andar jude to k ka kya hoga? Trap: forest wala formula har graph pe mat lagao.
dsa-graph-bfs-dist-05: Shortest paths ki **ginti** chahiye, sirf distance nahi. Ek vertex tak kai shortest paths aa sakte hain, jabki BFS tree sirf ek parent rakhta hai.
Pehle levels nikalo, phir paths(v) = sum of paths(u) over neighbours u jo exactly ek level upar hain. paths(A) = 1. Edges: A-B, A-C, A-E, B-D, B-F, C-G, D-H, E-F, F-H, G-H.
Levels: A 0; B, C, E 1; D, F, G 2; H 3. paths(B) = paths(C) = paths(E) = 1; ab D, F, G aur phir H nikalo. Trap: level-2 vertex ke saare level-1 neighbours gino, sirf tree parent nahi.
dsa-graph-bfs-dist-06: Graph **directed** hai — s se sirf edge ki direction mein chal sakte ho. f→s, g→b jaise edges s se kabhi use nahi honge.
BFS level by level: L1 = s ke out-neighbours, L2 = L1 ke out-neighbours jo pehle nahi mile. Sirf exactly distance 2 wale gino, usse kam wale nahi.
L1 = {a, b}. Ab a aur b ke out-edges se naye vertices nikalo — wahi L2 hai. Trap: e→a ko ulta use karke e ko distance 2 mat do.
dsa-graph-dfs-topo-01: Cross edge u→v: v already finished hai, pehle discover hua tha (d[v] < d[u]) aur u ka descendant nahi. Isliye poora DFS restart ke saath trace karna padega.
Scan pe classify karo: v new → tree; v open → back; v finished & d[u] < d[v] → forward; v finished & d[v] < d[u] → cross. Out-lists: a{b, c, d}, b{d}, c{d, e}, d{a}, e{b, c}, f{e, g}, g{f}.
a(1) → b(2) → d(3); d→a: a open hai → back edge. d, b finish. Ab a→c se aage chalo, phir f se restart. Trap: do trees ke beech wale edges bhi cross hote hain — unhe miss mat karo.
dsa-graph-dfs-topo-02: a→d ka type is pe depend karta hai ki jab a, d ko scan kare tab d ki state kya hai (new, open ya finished) aur dono ke discovery times kya hain.
a ki list alphabetical: b, c, d — to a→d sabse last scan hoga. Rule: finished & d[a] < d[d] → forward; finished & d[d] < d[a] → cross; open → back; new → tree.
a (d = 1) → b (2) → d (3): d pehle hi b ke through mil gaya aur finish ho gaya. Ab jab a, d ko scan kare, discovery times compare karo. Trap: d→a back edge hai, a→d nahi — direction dekho.
dsa-graph-dfs-topo-03: Char claims: directed cycle ↔ back edge, undirected DFS ke edge types, cross edge ke discovery times, aur DAG mein back edge. Har ek ko definition se check karo.
Back edge = open ancestor ki taraf edge, jo tree path ke saath cycle banata hai. Cross edge = finished vertex ki taraf jo descendant nahi. Undirected edge dono endpoints se scan ho sakta hai.
C test karo: cross edge u→v pe v already finished hai jab u abhi discover hua — to d[v] aur d[u] mein chhota kaun? D ke liye socho: back edge bina cycle ke ban sakta hai kya?
dsa-graph-dfs-topo-04: Kahn's algorithm: har step pe current in-degree 0 wale vertices mein se **alphabetically smallest** nikalo, phir uske out-edges hata ke in-degrees update karo.
Initial in-degrees: p 0, q 1, r 2 (p, u), s 2 (q, r), t 2 (s, v), u 0, v 1. Available set {p, u} se shuru karo.
Step 1: p nikalo → q ka in-degree 0, r ka 1. Available {q, u}. Ab aage karo. Trap: FIFO queue (discovery order) mat use karo — har baar smallest available lo.
dsa-graph-dfs-topo-05: DAG ke do alag parts hain: {a, b, c, d} aur {e, f}. Dono ke beech koi edge nahi, to unhe aapas mein kaise bhi interleave kar sakte ho.
Total = (part 1 ke valid orders) × (6 positions mein se e, f ki 2 positions choose karne ke tareeke; e hamesha f se pehle). Part 1 mein a first aur d last.
Part 1: a, phir b aur c kisi bhi order mein, phir d → 2 orders. Ab e, f ke liye 6 mein se 2 positions choose karo. Trap: e f ko ek block mat maano — adjacent hona zaroori nahi.
dsa-graph-dfs-topo-06: Ye DFS method hai, Kahn nahi: vertex **finish** hone pe list mein append hota hai, aur end mein list reverse hoti hai.
Out-lists alphabetical: p{q, r}, q{s}, r{s}, s{t}, u{r, v}, v{t}. p se DFS, phir smallest unvisited (u) se restart. Finish order likho, phir ulta karo.
p → q → s → t; t ka koi out-edge nahi, to pehle t finish, phir s, phir q. Ab p ke agle neighbour r se aage chalo. Trap: finishing order ko bina reverse kiye mat likho.
dsa-graph-dijkstra-01: Weighted shortest path chahiye — fewest edges wala path nahi, sabse kam total weight wala. Zyada hops wala path bhi sasta pad sakta hai (jaise s→b→a vs s→a).
Relaxation: $d[v] = \min(d[v], d[u] + w)$. Order mein nikalo: d[b], d[a], d[c], d[d], d[t] — har ek ke saare incoming options compare karke.
d[b] = 1, d[a] = min(4, 1 + 2) = 3. Ab d[c] = min(1 + 5, 3 + 1), phir d[d] aur d[t] khud nikalo. Trap: c→t (7) seedha mat lo — c→d→t bhi compare karo.
dsa-graph-dijkstra-02: Sirf d[d] ki value kitni baar strictly ghatti hai, wo gino — ∞ se pehli value bhi ek update hai. Extraction khud update nahi hai.
d ke incoming edges: b→d (8) aur c→d (3). d[d] tabhi badlega jab b ya c extract hoke relax kare aur nayi value purani se chhoti ho.
Extract s: d[a] = 4, d[b] = 1. Extract b (smallest): d[a] = 3, d[c] = 6, d[d] = 1 + 8 = 9 (pehla update). Ab aage extractions trace karo. Trap: d ke extract hone ko update mat gino.
dsa-graph-dijkstra-03: Sawaal ek snapshot ka hai: exactly 3 extractions (aur unke relaxations) ke baad, final distances nahi. Sirf extracted vertices apne edges relax karte hain.
Har step: unfinished vertices mein smallest d wala extract karo, uske out-edges relax karo. Teen extractions ke baad (d[c], d[d], d[t]) note karo.
Extract s (0): a = 4, b = 1. Extract b (1): a = 3, c = 6, d = 9. Ab teesra extraction kaun hai aur uske out-edges kya badalte hain? Trap: c→t abhi relax mat karo — c extract nahi hua.
dsa-graph-dijkstra-04: Ek negative edge b→a (-4) hai, par koi cycle nahi. Dijkstra extracted vertex ko dobara update nahi karta — dekho ye rule yahan kya bigaadta hai.
Do cheezein alag nikalo: (1) Dijkstra ka trace (smallest extract, relax, finalized vertex locked); (2) asli shortest distance, saare s→t paths ke weights compare karke.
Extract s: a = 2, b = 5. Extract a (2 < 5): c = 2 + 3 = 5. Ab b extract karo — b→a se a ko kya milta, aur kya a update hoga? Trap: negative edge ≠ negative cycle.
dsa-graph-dijkstra-05: Char claims: Dijkstra ki condition, Bellman-Ford ki condition, constant reweighting, aur Dijkstra with negative edges. Har ek ko uske rule se check karo.
Dijkstra ka greedy step tabhi safe hai jab koi edge negative na ho. Bellman-Ford n - 1 rounds mein har simple path cover karta hai; condition: koi reachable negative cycle na ho.
C test karo: P1 = ek edge weight 3, P2 = teen edges weight 1 each. Har edge mein +2 jodo — ab totals kya hain? D: ek negative edge (bina cycle) finalized vertex ke saath kya kar sakti hai?
